_note: Book-level background notes. status 'draft' = written with AI assistance, not yet reviewed. Keep wording neutral across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions; give dates as ranges and mark traditional attributions as such.

GEN.author: Traditionally attributed to Moses. Many scholars see several sources brought together over time.
GEN.date: Traditionally about 1400s BC; final form often dated to the 500s BC.
GEN.setting: From creation to Joseph in Egypt, across the ancient Near East.
GEN.purpose: To tell where the world, humanity and Israel came from, and how God began His promises to Abraham's family.

EXO.author: Traditionally attributed to Moses.
EXO.date: Traditionally about 1400s BC; final form later.
EXO.setting: Israel's slavery in Egypt, the escape, and the journey to Mount Sinai.
EXO.purpose: To show God rescuing His people and binding Himself to them by covenant, law and His presence in the tabernacle.

LEV.author: Traditionally attributed to Moses.
LEV.date: Traditionally about 1400s BC; final form later.
LEV.setting: At Mount Sinai, after the tabernacle is built.
LEV.purpose: To teach how a holy God can live among His people, through sacrifice, worship and daily holiness.

NUM.author: Traditionally attributed to Moses.
NUM.date: Traditionally about 1400s BC; final form later.
NUM.setting: Forty years in the wilderness between Sinai and the edge of Canaan.
NUM.purpose: To record Israel's journey, their failures of trust, and God's faithfulness to a new generation.

DEU.author: Traditionally attributed to Moses, with an account of his death added later.
DEU.date: Traditionally about 1400s BC; many scholars link its final form to the 600s BC.
DEU.audience: A new generation of Israel about to enter the land.
DEU.setting: The plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River.
DEU.purpose: To renew the covenant and call Israel to love God with all their heart.

JOS.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition names Joshua for most of it.
JOS.date: Events about 1400s to 1200s BC; written later.
JOS.setting: Israel crosses the Jordan and settles in Canaan.
JOS.purpose: To show God keeping His promise of the land, and to call Israel to serve Him alone.

JDG.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition names Samuel.
JDG.date: Events about 1200s to 1000s BC; written during or after the early monarchy.
JDG.setting: The years between Joshua and the first king, when Israel had no central leader.
JDG.purpose: To show the cycle of turning from God, suffering, crying out and rescue, and Israel's need for faithful leadership.

RUT.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition names Samuel.
RUT.date: Set in the time of the judges; written during the monarchy or later.
RUT.setting: Moab and the town of Bethlehem.
RUT.purpose: To tell of loyal love and God's quiet care, leading to the family line of King David.

1SA.author: Unknown. Drawn from the records of prophets such as Samuel, Nathan and Gad.
1SA.date: Events about 1100s to 1000s BC; compiled later.
1SA.setting: Israel moves from judges to kings: Samuel, Saul and young David.
1SA.purpose: To show what kind of king God wants, and how He chose David.

2SA.author: Unknown. Drawn from prophetic and court records.
2SA.setting: David's reign as king over Judah and then all Israel.
2SA.purpose: To record God's covenant with David and the cost of David's sins in his family and kingdom.

1KI.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition names Jeremiah.
1KI.date: Events about 970 to 850 BC; finished during the exile, after 560 BC.
1KI.audience: Israel, many of them in exile.
1KI.setting: Solomon's reign, the temple, and the split into two kingdoms.
1KI.purpose: To explain why the kingdom fell, measuring each king by faithfulness to God.

2KI.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition names Jeremiah.
2KI.date: Events about 850 to 560 BC; finished during the exile.
2KI.setting: The divided kingdoms until Israel falls to Assyria and Judah to Babylon.
2KI.purpose: To show that exile came from turning away from God, while keeping hope in His promise to David.

1CH.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition names Ezra.
1CH.audience: Jews who had returned from exile.
1CH.setting: Israel's history from Adam to David, retold after the exile.
1CH.purpose: To remind a returned people of their roots, of David, and of worship at the temple.

2CH.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition names Ezra.
2CH.audience: Jews who had returned from exile.
2CH.setting: From Solomon to the fall of Jerusalem and the decree of Cyrus.
2CH.purpose: To show that seeking God brings renewal, and to encourage faithful worship.

EZR.author: Traditionally attributed to Ezra.
EZR.audience: Jews who had returned to Judah.
EZR.setting: Return from Babylon and the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem.
EZR.purpose: To show God keeping His promise to bring His people home and renewing them by His word.

NEH.author: Largely Nehemiah's own memoir, with other material.
NEH.audience: Jews in Judah after the exile.
NEH.setting: Rebuilding Jerusalem's walls under Persian rule.
NEH.purpose: To record the city's restoration and the people's renewed commitment to God.

EST.author: Unknown.
EST.setting: The royal court of Persia at Susa. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include longer Greek additions.
EST.purpose: To tell how the Jews were saved from destruction, and to explain the feast of Purim.

JOB.author: Unknown.
JOB.audience: Readers wrestling with suffering and justice.
JOB.setting: The land of Uz, outside Israel, in the time of the patriarchs.
JOB.purpose: To explore why the righteous suffer, and to point to God's wisdom beyond human understanding.

PSA.author: Many writers, including David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and Moses.
PSA.date: Written over centuries, about 1400s to 400s BC.
PSA.audience: Israel at worship, and anyone who prays.
PSA.setting: Temple worship, personal crisis, exile and return.
PSA.purpose: To give words for praise, lament, trust and thanks before God.

PRO.author: Mainly Solomon, with sayings from others such as Agur and Lemuel.
PRO.date: About 900s BC, gathered over time into the 700s BC or later.
PRO.audience: The young and anyone seeking wisdom.
PRO.setting: Daily life: home, work, speech and community.
PRO.purpose: To teach practical wisdom rooted in the fear of the Lord.

ECC.author: “The Preacher” (Qoheleth), traditionally identified with Solomon.
ECC.date: Traditionally 900s BC; many scholars date it 400s to 200s BC.
ECC.purpose: To show that life without God is empty, and to point to fearing God and enjoying His gifts.

SNG.author: Traditionally attributed to Solomon.
SNG.audience: Israel; read in Jewish and Christian worship.
SNG.setting: Poems of love between a bride and her beloved.
SNG.purpose: To celebrate faithful love. Jewish and Christian traditions also read it as a picture of God's love for His people.

ISA.author: Isaiah son of Amoz. Many scholars think later chapters came from his followers.
ISA.date: Isaiah's ministry about 740 to 680 BC; later sections possibly 500s BC.
ISA.audience: Judah and Jerusalem, and later the exiles.
ISA.setting: The threat of Assyria, and later the exile in Babylon.
ISA.purpose: To call God's people to trust Him, warn of judgment, and promise comfort and a coming servant-king.

JER.author: Jeremiah, with his scribe Baruch.
JER.audience: Judah in its last years and the first exiles.
JER.setting: Jerusalem before and after its fall to Babylon.
JER.purpose: To call Judah to return to God, to explain the exile, and to promise a new covenant.

LAM.author: Unknown. Traditionally attributed to Jeremiah.
LAM.purpose: To grieve honestly before God while holding on to His faithful mercy.

EZK.author: Ezekiel, a priest and prophet.
EZK.setting: By the river Chebar in Babylon.
EZK.purpose: To explain why Jerusalem fell and to promise new hearts, new life and God's return.

DAN.author: Traditionally attributed to Daniel. Many scholars date the final form to the 160s BC.
DAN.audience: Jews living under foreign empires. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include additional Greek sections.
DAN.setting: The royal courts of Babylon and Persia.
DAN.purpose: To show God ruling over the nations and keeping His people faithful under pressure.

HOS.author: Hosea.
HOS.setting: Israel's last years before falling to Assyria.
HOS.purpose: To show God's faithful love for an unfaithful people, through Hosea's own marriage.

JOL.author: Joel.
JOL.date: Uncertain; proposals range from 800s to 400s BC.
JOL.setting: After a devastating plague of locusts.
JOL.purpose: To call the people to return to God and to promise the outpouring of His Spirit.

AMO.author: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa.
AMO.setting: A time of wealth, injustice and empty worship.
AMO.purpose: To demand justice and righteousness, and to warn of judgment.

OBA.author: Obadiah.
OBA.purpose: To announce judgment on Edom's pride and the restoration of God's people.

JON.author: Unknown; about Jonah son of Amittai.
JON.date: Set in the 700s BC; written later.
JON.setting: Jonah's flight and his mission to Nineveh in Assyria.
JON.purpose: To show God's mercy reaching even Israel's enemies.

MIC.author: Micah of Moresheth.
MIC.setting: The rise of Assyria, alongside Isaiah's ministry.
MIC.purpose: To warn against injustice and false worship, and to promise a ruler from Bethlehem.

NAM.author: Nahum.
NAM.setting: Before the fall of Nineveh, Assyria's capital.
NAM.purpose: To announce the end of a cruel empire and comfort God's people.

HAB.author: Habakkuk.
HAB.setting: Babylon's rise, just before it invades Judah.
HAB.purpose: To wrestle with God over injustice and to learn that the righteous live by faith.

ZEP.author: Zephaniah.
ZEP.purpose: To warn of the day of the Lord and promise joy for a humble remnant.

HAG.author: Haggai.
HAG.audience: Jews who had returned to Jerusalem.
HAG.setting: The rebuilding of the temple had stalled.
HAG.purpose: To call the people to finish God's house and trust His promises.

ZEC.author: Zechariah. Some scholars think later chapters came from a later writer.
ZEC.audience: Jews who had returned to Jerusalem.
ZEC.setting: The rebuilding of the temple after the exile.
ZEC.purpose: To encourage the people with visions of God's return and a coming king.

MAL.author: Malachi (the name means “my messenger”).
MAL.audience: Jews in Judah after the exile.
MAL.setting: The second temple stands, but worship has grown careless.
MAL.purpose: To call priests and people back to faithful worship and to promise a coming messenger.

MAT.author: Traditionally attributed to Matthew, the tax collector and apostle.
MAT.setting: The life of Jesus in Galilee and Judea.
MAT.purpose: To show that Jesus is the promised Messiah and to teach the way of His kingdom.

MRK.author: Traditionally attributed to John Mark, drawing on Peter's preaching.
MRK.audience: Mainly Gentile Christians, perhaps in Rome.
MRK.setting: The ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus.
MRK.purpose: To show that Jesus is the Son of God who came to serve and give His life.

LUK.author: Traditionally attributed to Luke, a physician and companion of Paul.
LUK.setting: The life of Jesus, from His birth to His ascension.
LUK.purpose: To give an orderly account of Jesus, the Savior for all people.

JHN.author: Traditionally attributed to John the apostle, “the disciple whom Jesus loved”.
JHN.audience: Believers and seekers, Jewish and Gentile.
JHN.setting: The ministry of Jesus, mostly in Judea and Jerusalem.
JHN.purpose: “That ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name” (John 20:31).

ACT.author: Traditionally attributed to Luke, the writer of the third Gospel.
ACT.setting: From Jerusalem to Rome, about AD 30 to 62.
ACT.purpose: To show the Holy Spirit spreading the good news of Jesus to the ends of the earth.

ROM.author: Paul the apostle.
ROM.audience: The church in Rome, Jewish and Gentile believers.
ROM.setting: Written from Corinth before Paul's visit to Jerusalem.
ROM.purpose: To explain the gospel: God's righteousness, grace and faith for Jew and Gentile alike.

1CO.author: Paul the apostle.
1CO.setting: Written from Ephesus to a gifted but divided church.
1CO.purpose: To correct divisions and disorder, and to teach love and the hope of resurrection.

2CO.author: Paul the apostle.
2CO.setting: Written from Macedonia after a painful season.
2CO.purpose: To defend Paul's ministry and show God's strength in human weakness.

GAL.author: Paul the apostle.
GAL.setting: Some taught that Gentile believers must keep the law of Moses.
GAL.purpose: To defend the gospel of grace and freedom in Christ.

EPH.author: Paul the apostle. Some scholars think a later follower wrote it.
EPH.date: About AD 60 to 62, during Paul's imprisonment.
EPH.audience: The church in Ephesus and nearby churches.
EPH.purpose: To show God's plan to unite all things in Christ, and how the Church lives that out.

PHP.author: Paul the apostle, with Timothy.
PHP.setting: Written from prison to a church Paul loved.
PHP.purpose: To thank them and call them to joy, unity and humility like Christ's.

COL.author: Paul the apostle, with Timothy.
COL.setting: Written from prison as false teaching spread.
COL.purpose: To show that Christ is supreme and enough.

1TH.author: Paul, with Silas and Timothy.
1TH.setting: Written from Corinth soon after the church began.
1TH.purpose: To encourage a persecuted church and teach about Christ's return.

2TH.author: Paul, with Silas and Timothy.
2TH.setting: Confusion had grown about the day of the Lord.
2TH.purpose: To correct that confusion and call believers to steady, faithful work.

1TI.author: Paul the apostle. Some scholars think a later follower wrote it.
1TI.audience: Timothy, leading the church in Ephesus.
1TI.setting: Instructions for church life and leadership.
1TI.purpose: To guide sound teaching, worship and leadership.

2TI.author: Paul the apostle. Some scholars think a later follower wrote it.
2TI.purpose: To urge Timothy to stay faithful and keep passing on the gospel.

TIT.author: Paul the apostle. Some scholars think a later follower wrote it.
TIT.setting: New churches needing order and leaders.
TIT.purpose: To show how sound teaching leads to good lives.

PHM.author: Paul the apostle.
PHM.audience: Philemon, a believer in Colossae, and his house church.
PHM.setting: Onesimus, who had left Philemon's household, had come to faith with Paul.
PHM.purpose: To ask Philemon to welcome Onesimus back as a brother.

HEB.author: Unknown. Paul, Barnabas and Apollos have been suggested.
HEB.audience: Jewish Christians tempted to turn back.
HEB.setting: A community under pressure and persecution.
HEB.purpose: To show that Jesus is greater than angels, Moses and the old priesthood, and to call readers to persevere.

JAS.author: Traditionally attributed to James, the brother of the Lord and leader in Jerusalem.
JAS.setting: Believers facing trials, poverty and favoritism.
JAS.purpose: To show that real faith shows itself in action.

1PE.author: Peter the apostle.
1PE.setting: Christians facing suffering for their faith.
1PE.purpose: To give hope in suffering and call believers to holy living.

2PE.author: Peter the apostle. Some scholars think a later follower wrote it.
2PE.audience: Believers, likely those who received 1 Peter.
2PE.purpose: To warn against false teaching and affirm Christ's return.

1JN.author: Traditionally attributed to John the apostle.
1JN.audience: Churches in the region of Ephesus.
1JN.setting: Some had left the community, denying Jesus came in the flesh.
1JN.purpose: To give assurance of eternal life and call believers to love one another.

2JN.author: “The elder”, traditionally John the apostle.
2JN.audience: “The elect lady and her children”, likely a local church.
2JN.purpose: To urge love, truth, and care about whom to welcome.

3JN.author: “The elder”, traditionally John the apostle.
3JN.setting: A church leader, Diotrephes, refused to welcome traveling teachers.
3JN.purpose: To commend Gaius's hospitality and encourage doing good.

JUD.author: Jude, brother of James.
JUD.audience: Believers under threat from false teachers.
JUD.setting: Ungodly people had slipped into the church.
JUD.purpose: To urge believers to contend for the faith and keep themselves in God's love.

REV.author: John, traditionally the apostle.
REV.date: About AD 95, or possibly the late 60s.
REV.setting: Written on the island of Patmos during persecution.
REV.purpose: To reveal Christ's victory and give hope that God will make all things new.
